title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Named Centerpiece of Tokyo Film Festival as ‘Sukiyaki’ Opens, ‘Colony’ Closes
description: “Godzilla Minus Zero” will screen as the centerpiece of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, with Zeze Takahisa’s music drama “Sukiyaki” open
body:
“Godzilla Minus Zero” will screen as the centerpiece of the 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, with Zeze Takahisa’s music drama “Sukiyaki” opening the festival and Yeon Sang-ho‘s zombie thriller “Colony” closing it.

	Director Yamazaki Takashi, who also wrote and oversaw visual effects on the film, returns with “Godzilla Minus Zero” as a follow-up to “Godzilla Minus One,” which won the Academy Award for best visual effects at the 96th Academy Awards. The film stars Kamiki Ryunosuke and Hamabe Minami and marks the first time a Japanese feature has been shot for Imax screens. Set two years after the events of the prior film, the story follows a Japan still struggling to recover when a new threat emerges. Festival materials frame it as the conclusion of the story that began with “Godzilla Minus One.” Toho Co., Ltd. will release the film in Japan on Nov. 3.
	

	In a statement, Ichiyama Shozo, TIFF programming director, said “Godzilla Minus Zero” is “a true sequel to ‘Godzilla Minus One,’ one of the standouts in the Godzilla series, and it brings a powerful new interpretation of Godzilla, delivering a level of surprise that far exceeds expectations.”


	“Sukiyaki,” directed by Zeze Takahisa from a screenplay by Minato Takehiko, chronicles the making of the 1963 song “Sukiyaki,” which held the No. 1 spot on the U.S. Billboard chart for three consecutive weeks. The film centers on composer Nakamura Hachidai, lyricist Ei Rokusuke and singer Sakamoto Kyu, played respectively by Okada Junichi, Matsuzaka Tori and Nakano Taiga. Toho will release the film in Japan on Dec. 25.
	

	Ichiyama said “Sukiyaki” tells “the dramatic stories of three artists who inspired people in postwar Japan, interwoven with a collection of musical masterpieces.” He added that TIFF is “delighted to open the festival with this moving film, which stars three of today’s most prominent Japanese actors.”

	“Colony” is directed by Yeon Sang-ho, whose credits include “Train to Busan” (2016). The Korean zombie thriller follows Professor Se Jeong, who becomes trapped in a Seoul skyscraper during a bioterror attack and witnesses infected hosts evolving with a collective intelligence. The cast includes Gianna Jun, Koo Kyo-hwan and Ji Chang-wook. The film had its world premiere in a Cannes midnight screening before topping box office charts in Korea and elsewhere in Asia. Gaga Corporation will distribute the film in Japan in 2027.

	Ichiyama called “Colony” the film that “delivered the greatest excitement and emotional impact among the films at this year’s Cannes,” adding that while zombie films are common, “this film makes us realize that the genre still possesses untapped potential.”

	The 39th Tokyo International Film Festival, hosted by Unijapan, runs Oct. 26 to Nov. 4 in Tokyo. The festival overlaps with TIFFCOM 2026, an industry market organized by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, and Unijapan, running Oct. 28-30.

schema.headline: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Named Centerpiece of Tokyo Film Festival as ‘Sukiyaki’ Opens, ‘Colony’ Closes

title: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Season 2 Sets François Arnaud, Robbie G.K., Sophie Nélisse and More Returning Cast Members
description: François Arnaud and Robbie G.K. will reprise their roles as Scott and Kip for the second season of “Heated Rivalry,” joining Connor Storrie and Huds
body:
François Arnaud and Robbie G.K. will reprise their roles as Scott and Kip for the second season of “Heated Rivalry,” joining Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams for the hockey drama. 

	Returning alongside Arnaud and G.K. for the sophomore season are Sophie Nélisse as Rose, Ksenia Daniela Kharlamova as Svetlana, Callan Potter as Hayden and Benjamin Roy as JJ. Kamilla Kowal will reprise her role as Hayden’s wife, Jackie, alongside Christina Chang and Dylan Walsh as Shane’s parents. 
	

	Previously announced cast members for Season 2 include Justice Smith as Harris, Charlie Gillespie as Troy, Daniel Diemer as Ryan, Shaheen Jafargholi as Fabian, Emily Hampshire as Vanessa, Edvin Ryding as Luca, Robert Naylor as Wyatt, Sabrina Jalees as Farah and Priyanka as Tarek.


	Season 2 adapts the second book in Rachel Reid’s “Game Changers” series “The Long Game,” which sees Shane and Ilya 10 years after their relationship began. The second season will also feature elements from Reid’s fifth book, “Role Model.” 

	Smith and Gillespie will lead the sophomore season alongside Storrie and Williams, who had their breakout roles in Season 1 as Ilya Rozanov and Shane Hollander, respectively. The first season followed hockey players Ilya and Shane, who began a secret fling that ultimately turned into a “years-long journey of love, denial and self-discovery,” per the season’s logline. 

	“Heated Rivalry” is created by Jacob Tierney, who also serves as writer, director and executive producer. The series is produced by Accent Aigu Entertainment in association with Bell Media’s Crave, with Brendan Brady and Jayme Alter Wilson executive producing. Lori Fischburg and Liane Cunje are producers alongside Reid, who serves as consulting producer. Mike Goldbach co-wrote Season 2.

schema.headline: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Season 2 Sets François Arnaud, Robbie G.K., Sophie Nélisse and More Returning Cast Members

title: Owner of L.A. Rams and Denver Nuggets Buys Los Angeles Angels Baseball Team
description: Kroenke Sports and Entertainment has acquired a majority stake in the Los Angeles Angels, adding a Major League Baseball franchise to a list of spor
body:
Kroenke Sports and Entertainment has acquired a majority stake in the Los Angeles Angels, adding a Major League Baseball franchise to a list of sports assets that includes the Los Angeles Rams, Denver Nuggets and Colorado Avalanche.

	Financial details of the deal were not immediately clear. Kroenke Sports is acquiring a majority interest from longtime owner Arte Moreno in a deal that should be completed in the first quarter of next year, pending approval from Major League Baseball. 
	

	The Angels have been on the market for some time. Moreno, the former owner of outdoor advertising giant Outdoor Systems, acquired the team from Disney in 2003. 


	With the Kroenke deal, the Angels will plug into a much larger sports and media ecosystem that should benefit the team that has always played down the road in Orange County in the shadow of the region’s beloved Los Angeles Dodgers franchise.

	“The Angels are a storied franchise anchored in a great market. We look forward to an exciting future with the Angels organization,” said E. Stanley Kroenke, owner and chairman of Kroenke Sports & Entertainment.

	Moreno’s regime has run afoul of many fans who complain about a lack of investment in the team. Moreno first initiated a sale process for the team in 2022. 

	“The Angels Organization is pleased to announce this transaction with Kroenke Sports & Entertainment. The Moreno Family has been honored to steward the Angels for 23 years and we believe with KSE’s experience and success they are the best next owner for the franchise. The Angels Organization looks forward to continuing its commitment to the fans, our employees, the players and our business partners,” Moreno said in a statement.
	

	In 2003, as the Angels came off an improbable World Series win in 2002, Moreno bought the team for about $185 million. At the time Disney was looking to shed non-core assets to focus on its core studio and theme park operations.

	Kroenke Sports noted that its considerable footprint in Southern California sports includes not only the Rams but SoFi Stadium and the 300-acre Hollywood Park district in Inglewood, Calif. The goal is to turn the area into a sports and entertainment corridor that will host Olympic and Paralympic events in 2028.

	Under Moreno, the team that had been the Anaheim Angels changed their moniker to the Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim in 2005. By 2016, the team dropped the “of Anaheim.” Per MLB, the team began its life in 1961 as the Los Angeles Angels. In 1965, the team began a 32-year run as the California Angels before shifting in 1997 to the Anaheim Angels.

	(Pictured: Angels’ pitcher Walbert Urena on the mound at Anaheim Stadium on Aug. 31)

schema.headline: Owner of L.A. Rams and Denver Nuggets Buys Los Angeles Angels Baseball Team

title: Tubi Sets Short-Form Horror Anthology Series ‘Bite Size Terror’ For Fall Release (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Tubi has unveiled the new short-form horror anthology “Bite Size Terror,” from executive producer Peter Rice and GJMD Studio. The 10-episode series
body:
Tubi has unveiled the new short-form horror anthology “Bite Size Terror,” from executive producer Peter Rice and GJMD Studio. The 10-episode series debuts as part of the Terror on Tubi Hub in fall 2026. 

	According to an official description, “Bite Size Terror” covers “every corner” of the horror genre, “from the supernatural and occult to body horror, dark comedy, monsters and the macabre.” Across the debut season, themes like “grief, ambition, intimacy and vulnerability become entry points for something darker, as characters searching for connection, control, or a way forward find themselves confronting forces they do not understand.” 
	

	“Bite Size Terror” is the latest effort in Tubi’s robust push toward short-form offerings. In 2024, the streamer launched “Scenes,” a scrollable TikTok-esque feed of snippets from Tubi’s library of TV shows and movies. Clipified content as a way to compete with social media and YouTube is only just catching on at the major streamers, with Netflix, Prime Video and HBO Max all jumping on the bandwagon in 2026. Tubi has also long partnered with digital creators by platforming their content. In some cases, those contracts are free of exclusivity barriers. 


	“With a different nightmare in every episode, ‘Bite Size Terror’ is a thrilling showcase for the next generation of horror filmmakers,” said Adam Lewinson, Chief Content Officer at Tubi. “It brings bold, unpredictable stories to the Terror on Tubi Hub, adding to an already compelling destination for fans with more than 53 million hours of horror to explore. We’re proud to partner with Peter, David and GJMD to bring these distinctive new voices directly to our audience.”
	

	“Our horror shorts have become an extraordinary engine for discovering new writer-directors, 90 shorts, nine first features and counting”,  added Rice. “We’re thrilled to partner with Tubi to introduce the next generation of horror filmmakers, with ‘Bite Size Terror’ on Tubi”. 

	“Bite Size Terror” is produced by GJMD studio, and executive produced by Rice, David Worthen Brooks, Arbi Pedrossian and David Moore. The deal was brokered by David Worthen Brooks and Lewinson.

schema.headline: Tubi Sets Short-Form Horror Anthology Series ‘Bite Size Terror’ For Fall Release (EXCLUSIVE)

title: ‘GTA 6’ Extended Look Tops Netflix Charts With 31.1 Million Views in Four Days
description: With only six hours of exclusivity before it hit YouTube, Netflix’s “Grand Theft Auto 6” extended look became the streamer’s most-viewed title last
body:
With only six hours of exclusivity before it hit YouTube, Netflix’s “Grand Theft Auto 6” extended look became the streamer’s most-viewed title last week. 

	Between its release on Thursday, Aug. 27 at 3 p.m. ET and Sunday, Aug. 30 (the end of Netflix’s viewing window for its weekly Top 10 rankings) the 27-minute “GTA 6” special drew 31.1 million views. 

	The extended look at the highly anticipated Rockstar Games title, which marks an entirely new category of entertainment for Netflix, was classified under the English-language film list for the week. It was No. 1 on that list in 87 of 93 countries that Netflix tracks globally.
	

	For comparison, the “Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look” viewed has topped 17 million views on YouTube, as of the time of publication Tuesday. The video was posted to YouTube by Rockstar Games at 9 p.m. ET last Thursday, following its exclusive debut earlier that day on Netflix.

	It should be noted here that YouTube and Netflix count views very differently. Netflix defines a view as the total hours viewed for a title divided by its runtime, meaning one household watching a program twice would be counted only once. On YouTube, a view is counted as soon as any video (whether its a short, a repeat viewing or partial plays) starts to play.

	The “Grand Theft Auto VI: An Extended Look” content was captured entirely from in-game footage on PlayStation 5 (the game will be released for PS5 and Xbox Series X and S on Nov. 19), per Netflix and Take-Two Interactive-owned publisher Rockstar. It marks the lengthiest look fans have gotten at “GTA 6” thus far, following two trailers released over the past three years.
	

	The special features “GTA 6” protagonists Jason and Lucia in both cinematic and gameplay scenes throughout the fictional Vice City, and teases the overall narrative of the game.

	Coming in at a distant second on the Top 10 English-language movies list was “The Whisper Man” with 23.2 million views.

	On the TV side, the documentary “Death of the Pastor’s Wife” was No. 1 with 19 million views, while the third season of Tyler Perry’s “Beauty in Black” was runnerup with 13 million views.

	See the full Netflix Top 10 rankings for the week here.

schema.headline: ‘GTA 6’ Extended Look Tops Netflix Charts With 31.1 Million Views in Four Days

title: Music Industry Moves: BMG-Concord Merger Is Complete, New Executive Teams Announced
description:
BMG has announced its executive management team and strategic leadership council, following the completion of its merger with Concord.

	Working und
body:
BMG has announced its executive management team and strategic leadership council, following the completion of its merger with Concord.

	Working under the oversight of BMG’s board of directors, the executive team will be comprised of the following individuals:

	Bob Valentine, Chief Executive OfficerBjörn Bauer, Chief Financial OfficerSebastian Hentzschel, Chief Operating OfficerVictor Zaraya, Chief Revenue OfficerAmanda Molter, General CounselKent Hoskins, Chief Transformation Officer
	

	BMG has also established an 18-member strategic leadership council, comprising the six members of the executive management team and 12 additional senior leaders from across the company (listed below). 


	Tom Becci, Global Recorded OperationsAlberto Chullen, Corporate Development & InvestmentsSophia Dilley, Concord OriginalsSean Flahaven, Concord TheatricalsCeline Joshua, Global Marketing & StreamingNitsa Kalispera, Global Supply Chain OperationsJon Loba, Global Frontline RecordingsRuth Martinez, Human ResourcesKristal McKanders Dube, Corporate CommunicationsAlistair Norbury, Senior Creative Advisor to CEO Bob ValentineTom Scherer, Global Catalog RecordingsJim Selby, Global Music Publishing

	Further leadership appointments across BMG’s business and functions will be announced separately.

	Monday, August 31

	Japanese superstar singer-songwriter Yoshiki has signed a global distribution and publishing administration agreement with BMG through his record label, Melodee.

	BMG will provide global distribution for Yoshiki’s new releases, beginning with “Forever Love (Live),” his new collaboration with internationally celebrated vocalist Josh Groban. The agreement also encompasses his solo album “Eternal Melody” and X Japan albums released from 1993 onward, including the hit albums “Art of Life” and “Dahlia.” BMG will additionally administer his publishing outside Japan.
	

	Yoshiki said, “I’ve always believed that music has no borders. I’m now entering one of the most ambitious and creative chapters of my career, with new projects that bring together rock, pop, classical and contemporary music in ways I have never explored before. I’m thrilled to partner with BMG to bring this vision to the world. ‘Forever Love’ with Josh Groban marks the beginning-but this partnership represents something much bigger for the future.”

	“Yoshiki is a true global artist whose creativity, vision, and connection with fans transcend genres and borders,” said BMG senior VP Michael Kachko. “We are proud to partner with him at BMG to support and amplify this next chapter on a worldwide scale.”

	+ Concord Music Publishing has signed Israeli singer-songwriter-producer Noga Erez to an exclusive global publishing agreement. The company has also signed Erez’s partner and main collaborator Ori Rousso.

	The go-forward publishing agreement covers all future works as well as select key tracks from Erez’s catalogue, including “Stuck In Heaven,” “Bubbling,” “Penny Lame,” “Not My Problem” and recent single “I Love You” featuring Armani White.

	“Noga Erez is a force of nature and truly one of a kind,” says Adrian Hillekamp, director of A&R at Concord Music Publishing in Berlin. The music of Noga and Ori demands attention, their live show is beyond exhilarating and they keep innovating on every record. At the same time, they selflessly give energy, motivation and hope through their songs. It is a testament to their ability to inspire and a privilege for us to be a part of.”

	+ City of Hope, one of the largest and most advanced cancer research and treatment organizations in the U.S., has named Black Music Action Coalition president-CEO Willie “Prophet” Stiggers to the executive board of the Music, Film and Entertainment Industry group, Over the past five decades, the group has raised more than $180 million to support the organization’s work.

	“For more than five decades, MFEI has brought together people who have reached the highest levels of the entertainment business and want to use that influence for something larger than themselves,” said Kristin Bertell, City of Hope’s chief philanthropy officer. “Prophet is a natural addition to that tradition. He has built an extraordinary platform by bringing people together around issues that matter, and he understands the impact this industry can have when its leaders rally behind City of Hope’s mission to make hope a reality for all who face cancer.”

schema.headline: Music Industry Moves: BMG-Concord Merger Is Complete, New Executive Teams Announced

title: Chinese Feature ‘Big Little Things’ Turns a Real-Life Family Rift Into a Coming-Out Drama Now Headed for Venice Horizons (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The director-producer duo Michelle Zhou and Chun Yu collectively incubated “Big Little Things,” a lesbian coming-out story inspired by a real-life f
body:
The director-producer duo Michelle Zhou and Chun Yu collectively incubated “Big Little Things,” a lesbian coming-out story inspired by a real-life family rift during a New Year holiday amid the COVID-19 pandemic in Harbin, a snowy city in northern China.

	Zhou notes that the film was selected for the Venice Days first but was later invited by the Horizons. “We had to turn down the Venice Days even though we really love [ANAC and 100autori, the groups behind the section],” says Zhou. “It was a happy dilemma.”
	

	The film’s story stemmed from Zhou and Yu’s real-life family conflict, tracing back to four and a half years ago when they started dating.


	“During that time, [Yu] really wanted to share our happiness with her parents, and at the same time, she was terrified of losing them,” Zhou says. Since same-sex relationships have long been a social taboo in China, Yu told her family that Zhou was her friend and colleague.

	Nevertheless, Yu’s parents deduced that Zhou was actually Yu’s romantic partner, and the family collapsed overnight.

	“I was in deep family chaos. It was totally dark, I couldn’t do anything,” Yu tells Variety. “It was a difficult time not just for me, but also my parents because they had to learn about this new thing.”

	“I came from Harbin, and in our northeast Chinese culture, we say love and family expectations are inseparable. But when conflicts like that occur, most people would choose silence and lies to preserve the harmony,” says Zhou, who observed this turmoil from the sidelines. “That experience made me think, ‘Why do we have to lie to be close with the people we love? And why can honesty feel more dangerous than deception?’”
	

	After using the story as a base for a short film of the same name, Zhou expanded it into a feature to illuminate societal and heteronormative pressure through a fictional scenario — a fake boyfriend is introduced to appease the matchmaking-obsessed family, indicating the prevalence of lavender marriages in the Chinese LGBTQ+ community.

	“When we walk our dogs in the [neighborhood], gay people who knew us as lesbian would ask us if we could fake marry each other,” says Yu. “A lot of people are 100% sure that no matter what they tell their families, they will never accept that.”

	While addressing minority stress within the family, the film coincidentally summoned unexpected support — the father’s role was played by its real-life inspiration, Yu’s father, Hai.

	“My dad was in my [short] film before, so I know he could act,” says Yu. “I said, ‘We are looking for the father role, do you want to come?’ My father said, ‘If you can’t find someone else, you can come to ask me.’ And I said, ‘This is the moment I’m asking you: I need your help.’ A week later, he arrived in Harbin for the table read.”

	As Hai opened his heart on set while filming the emotional father-daughter confession scene, the profound pain was soothed. “He turned his back to everyone and sobbed, and said: ‘You don’t understand the feeling of a father losing his daughter,’” Yu confides. “He told me that he [took] the role because he wanted to rescue himself, and express everything he had not said in real life.”

	The director-producer duo will continue to collaborate on future projects. Zhou’s next feature, “Another Stranger,” is a family comedy-drama based on her experience with her cousin when they were trapped in Thailand during a trip due to the COVID lockdown from January to April 2020.

	“I was trying to understand our family from a different perspective. My cousin and I used to be very close when we were little, but during that period, he was not the man I used to know and I was not the woman he used to know. There was a lot of jealousy, vulnerability, masculinity — all these things mixed together on this tropical island,” Zhou says.

	A writer-director as well, Yu is working on her debut feature, a Chinese diaspora story set to take place in Los Angeles and a European village. The project is hitting international film markets, seeking American and European producers.
	

	Watch the trailer: https://youtu.be/0v-cCIKet28

schema.headline: Chinese Feature ‘Big Little Things’ Turns a Real-Life Family Rift Into a Coming-Out Drama Now Headed for Venice Horizons (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Venice Chief Alberto Barbera on the Fest’s Lineup Missing Israeli Films: ‘We Have No Prejudice Against Anyone Anywhere in the World’
description: Venice Film Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera spoke candidly Tuesday about the political pressures surrounding this year’s edition, while m
body:
Venice Film Festival artistic director Alberto Barbera spoke candidly Tuesday about the political pressures surrounding this year’s edition, while making clear that the fest has no intention of shying away from controversy.

	Speaking to Variety at the press cocktail on the Lido ahead of the 83rd edition, Barbera said it was “almost normal” that Venice was being pressed to take a political position given the number of films in the lineup touching on Gaza, Palestine, Ukraine and other contentious subjects.
	

	“There are several films that can start controversies or, at the very least, provoke very strong political reactions,” Barbera said. “They ask whether the festival — and especially the Biennale — is going to take very clear and explicit political positions. What we always say is that neither the Biennale nor the festival will make political declarations in order to take sides.”


	His comments came a day after Venice reinstated its jury press conference amid some backlash and as artists and activists, including Venice4Palestine, have called on the Biennale to take a stronger position on the war in Gaza.

	“We are a space for freedom of expression. Our role is to safeguard freedom of expression for everyone, for the artists, and to safeguard the confrontation between artists and the public, the critics and people in general,“ said Barbera. “We will never take an explicit political position. It doesn’t make any sense.”

	Barbera also firmly denied that the absence of Israeli films from this year’s lineup reflected a boycott, saying Venice received only one Israeli submission and chose not to invite it.
	

	“No, not at all. Never,” he said. “We have no prejudice against anyone anywhere in the world. If there had been a Russian film, an Israeli film of good quality, we would undoubtedly have invited it.”

	He added that Venice would have been prepared to face the political backlash that might have followed.

	Barbera also said the festival almost selected Vincent Gallo’s latest film, “Golden State Killer” starring James Franco, which Barbera revealed nearly made the lineup.

	“We told him, ‘We like the film very much. We know it is a film that is going to divide the public, but we are ready to face a complicated situation,’” Barbera said. Venice offered the film an out-of-competition berth, but Gallo ultimately declined because he wanted to compete for the Golden Lion. Asked whether Franco’s presence was a concern, Barbera said it was not, adding that the issue was the provocative nature of the film itself.

	Barbera, who has selected Roman Polanski’s and Woody Allen’s movies in recent years, said Venice could get away with these bold choices where other festivals would be plagued by a widespread scandal due to “the prestige of the Biennale and the credibility that the Biennale has gained over the years” through its defense of artistic freedom “without ever taking a political side.”

	Asked whether Allen might return with his next movie, which he’s about to shoot in Madrid, Barbera quipped: “It depend how good his next film will be! We’ll see. Maybe.”

	He also rejected the idea that Hollywood studios were retreating from Venice, saying several major U.S. titles simply were not ready in time, including films from Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher.

	“We know the situation in Hollywood. We know the situation of the studios. They are in difficulty,” he said, pointing to mergers and shifting production and distribution strategies.

	Still, Barbera predicted the studios would return, calling Venice “a very good promotional opportunity.”

	Venice opens Wednesday with “Ink,“ Danny Boyle’s drama about the birth of Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid empire, starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy.

	Why does everyone seem to want Venice to take a political position this year? 

	Because we had Berlin, obviously, with all the problems between the government, Palestine, the pro-Palestinian protests and all of that. Poor Wim Wenders was basically trapped by the press conference. At Cannes, a little less, because there weren’t really films that were politically very sensitive. Here, we have a lot of films. We have four films dealing with Gaza and Palestine. We have the problems of Ukraine. We have Elon Musk. There are several films that can start controversies or, at the very least, provoke very strong political reactions. So I would say it is almost normal that people expect something. They ask whether the festival — and especially the Biennale — is going to take very clear and explicit political positions. What we always say is that neither the Biennale nor the festival will make political declarations in order to take sides. Obviously, that is not what we do.
	

	But they are actually asking you to do that?

	Yes, they are asking us. For example, you know that the pro-Palestinian groups sent a document — the letter — asking for an official pro-Palestinian declaration and all of that. But after all, we are a space for freedom of expression. We invite films. We understand that there will be discussions, debates and everything that comes with that. Our role is to safeguard freedom of expression for everyone, for the artists, and to safeguard the confrontation between artists and the public, the critics and people in general. We will never take an explicit political position. It doesn’t make any sense.

	But at the same time, I think it is clear what our position is, because through the program, through the programming of the festival and through the films that we invite, it is clear what we are doing and what kind of space we want the festival to be.

	But you don’t have any Israeli films this year, do you?

	No.

	Why is that?

	First of all, because we received only one Israeli film. One single Israeli submission. We didn’t like it enough, so we decided not to invite it. And for the first time, we didn’t receive any other proposals for Israeli films. I don’t know why.

	So there is no boycott?

	No, not at all. Never. It is absolutely important to say that we have no prejudice against anyone anywhere in the world. If there had been a Russian film, an Israeli film of good quality, we would undoubtedly have invited it. And we were ready to face the political reaction that would have been predictable. Because if we had had an Israeli film, obviously the pro-Palestinian groups could have launched an international appeal to boycott the Israeli film and everything around it. That would have been horrible, but we were ready to face that situation.

	At one point, apparently you almost took the Vincent Gallo film with James Franco. What happened there?

	Yes and Vincent told us in the end that he preferred that we not do anything. He only wanted to come if he was in competition.

	Really?

	We told him, “We like the film very much. We know it is a film that is going to divide the public, but we are ready to face a complicated situation.” But not in competition, because we didn’t think the profile of the film would benefit from the competition. In the end, we discussed it a lot — a lot, for a long time — and finally he said: “No, I prefer not to come.”
	

	Was it a film that would have created controversy because of the film itself, or because of Vincent Gallo and James Franco?

	No, because of the film. Because of the subject.

	Because it is about a serial killer? Because it makes the serial killer sympathetic?

	No, but you know, with Vincent Gallo there is always an approach that is, let’s say, troubling. There is always something unsettling in the way he approaches a subject.

	But James Franco as well — wasn’t that a concern?

	No. We didn’t care about that. Because it has already been several years since James Franco fell somewhat off the radar. He has started making films again in Italy recently. There are at least two films that have come out without any particular negative reaction toward him. So we were not concerned because of his presence in the film. That wasn’t the issue for us.

	It seems that at Venice you can get away with things that at Cannes would immediately spark a huge backlash from journalists, the industry and everyone else. Why do you think Venice can do that?

	Why Venice? I think because of the prestige of the Biennale and the credibility that the Biennale has gained over the years through its international positioning and through decisions that people have appreciated. It has built this credibility through its defense of artistic freedom and everything that goes with that, without ever taking a political side.

	You have previously had Polanski, you have had Woody Allen. Could Woody Allen come back here with his next film?

	It depends how good his next film will be! We’ll see. Maybe.

	There are a lot of French and Italian films and filmmakers coming this year, but there are fewer Americans. Do you think the Americans will come back?

	I think they will. The problem was that there simply weren’t films for Venice. The only film that was ready was Iñárritu’s film with Tom Cruise (“Digger”). And they had the right to decide not to show the film at a festival, to release the film more or less everywhere in the world and to play on the surprise and on Tom Cruise’s ability to bring in an audience. It is a shame, obviously. I would have loved to have the film. But that was really the only film that was available, because the other films weren’t ready. Sorkin had to reshoot scenes in August, so his film (“The Social Reckoning”) wasn’t ready. David Fincher was delayed in post-production (with “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth”). There were simply no other films available for Venice.
	

	Are the studios also afraid of going to festivals like Venice because the critical reaction can be so tough?

	We know the situation in Hollywood. We know the situation of the studios. They are in difficulty. They are going through mergers. We don’t know how all of that is going to end. They are also rethinking their production strategies and their distribution strategies for films. So it is not a very good moment. There simply weren’t films ready at this particular moment. But I am sure that in the future the festival will continue to be an extraordinary opportunity for the promotion of films.

	But it’s expensive to come to Venice.

	It is not expensive. It depends, obviously, but if you have a film that costs $200 million and the studio is spending $5 million or much more on promoting the film, then coming to Venice or Cannes might cost around $1 million. Not more than that. So it is a very good promotional opportunity. I am sure they will come back.

title: Why Stella Lefty’s ‘Boston’ Became the Biggest Musical Punching Bag of the Decade — and One of the Biggest Songs of the Year
description: “I like it when you’re nice to me,” Stella Lefty sings in the hook of her breakthrough single, “Boston.” To which we can only reply right now: Hope
body:
“I like it when you’re nice to me,” Stella Lefty sings in the hook of her breakthrough single, “Boston.” To which we can only reply right now: Hope you’re not reading the comments.

	Try to recall the last time there was as much mass derision directed at one song as there is currently aimed at “Boston.” Would it have been back during quarantine, when Gal Gadot made everyone quesy with a highly mockable all-star cover of “Imagine”? Was it when Oliver Anthony became a quick cultural blip for his ingenious idea to fat-shame welfare recipients? Or would it have been when Jason Aldean was looking to make lynching cool again with “Try This in a Small Town”? But no, not even these examples approach the level of sheer enmity being laid upon what, on the surface, feels like as light-hearted and innocuous a single as anything any pop or country artist ever put down.
	

	Lefty is as close as we get to a true overnight sensation… and also a near-overnight scapegoat. She is going to be punished for all of America’s sins, and also get a bunch of platinum certifications and possibly a couple of Grammy nominations, before this ride is all over. If she still has her head on her shoulders at the end of it all, then it might mark one of the most striking psychological survival stories since Monica Lewinsky came out OK after all. Because the feeding frenzy is staggering.


	Of course, the pile-on feels even more justified to those inclined because everyone imagines Lefty crying — or being shamed — all the way to the bank. Because “Boston” is still looking like a Teflon hit, despite it seeming to make the entirety of the internet feel scorny. This week, it holds on yet again at No. 2 on the Hot 100, held back from the top spot only by Ella Langley’s indomitable, record-breaking “Choosin’ Texas,” which some would say paved the way, with the cement still wet, for “Boston.” There is a big part of the nation — maybe even a silent majority? — that’s just indifferent to or unaware of the fact that fellow citizens are being driven to paroxyms of deep sarcasm or rage by the song’s existence, and by the privilege they see in Lefty’s meteoric rise.
	

	Those not chronically online may at this point be asking: Why they gotta be so mean?

	Even prior to the release of “Boston,” when she was having a minor viral breakout with the song “Thinking ’bout You,” the 24-year-old singer began drawing some negative attention for the fact that she is the daughter of a billionaire. A six-times-over billionaire, to be exact, Groupon co-founder and Tempus AI CEO Eric Lefkofsky. Given that Lefty was plying her talent in a country or at least country-adjacent space, it was inevitable that a wealthy Illinoisan would face some thoughts along the lines of “I don’t think Hank done it that way.” Among people who don’t know country well enough to quote Waylon Jennings, the operative phrase was two of the most annoying words in the English language: “industry plant.” There was just one problem with the whisper campaign to bring Lefty’s career to an early halt: People loved “Boston”! Or a big portion of the mass public did, and they didn’t care that Lefty hadn’t had to work two waitress jobs to afford guitar lessons when her new signature song was this catchy and brought them that much joy.

	But then came an obvious big reason it was catchy and brought joy: a key part of the chorus bore an unmistakable resemblance to Noah Kahan‘s “Stick Season.” And not in the way where Sam Smith’s hit sounded a little like Tom Petty’s, or that Olivia Rodrigo was made to credit Taylor Swift because of a shared shoutiness. More in the kind of way where, once you became aware of the Lefty/Kahan similiarity, it was impossible to unhear it. Did that stand in the way of continuing to enjoy “Boston” for what it was — as a song that was at least a little bit delightful on its own terms? Yes, for some, and obviously not a big problem for others, with the song now approaching 300 million on-demand streams. But in the part of the public that thinks a great deal about egalitarianism and morality in music, Lefty had gone from “nepo” to “klepto” in one fell swoop, and now was being thought of by her antagonists as some kind of actual robber baron.

	Probably everyone could agree that Lefty had not done herself many favors when it came to countering the idea that she had borrowed her best melodic idea. Credit was given to Kahan as a co-writer on the track, but that seemed to be at the instigation of his camp, once the song started going viral from her socials before its official release. When Lefty was asked about the apparently accidental Kahan “interpolation” in a Vanity Fair interview, she replied, “When I was writing the song, I wasn’t thinking about Noah Kahan. I was literally thinking about nothing at all.” There are two serious problems with that answer: (1) Everyone who just thinks the song is banal quote-tweets it with the response, “We know.” (2) Evidence started mounting that Lefty seemed to have spent a good portion of her adult life thinking about Noah Kahan.
	

	Suddenly much of the web went into prosecuting attorney mode. Because Lefty had spent years leading up to this building her brand by posting acoustic covers of established hits, as singer-songwriters of her generation are encouraged to do, she had left a long digital trail of Kahan adoration — not just posting how she would do anything to earn his attention but repeatedly putting up covers of “Stick Season.” Speaking of sticky, someone put together a mega-montage of her different versions of his signature song from the past few years, to the point that you could imagine that if Lefty truly wasn’t thinking about Kahan when she wrote “Boston,” it must’ve been one of the few times she wasn’t.

	Evidence for the would-be prosecution accumulated further still when it came out that Lefty had given credit to the writers of the Dixie Chicks’ breakthrough hit “There’s Your Trouble” for an interpolaton of that song’s melody in her album track “Summer You Were Mine.” (Rolling Stone established that the credit had accidentally been left off for streaming services, but it had always been legally credited and intended, and the oversight was being rectified.) Needless to say, given the current unwanted attention, “Summer You Were Mine” will undoubtedly not be a follow-up single for Lefty.

	Who knows what was really going through Lefty’s or her team’s minds as “Boston” started to take off, knowing that it was a minefield laden with gold and platinum? It may be possible that the young singer had “Stick Season” so ingrained into every fabric of her being that she wasn’t consciously copying the tune, and that once she let the public hear it before very much of the music industry had, it was too big a juggernaut to pull back. Co-crediting Kahan was the most obvious — and completely unavoidable — step to take in rectifying the situation. Admitting she had at least a subliminal influence, rather than claiming a brain with a completely blank slate, would have gone further in forestalling her current public-relations crisis.

	One side benefit of the Lefty kerfuffle is the renewal of the eternal conversation over what constitutes plagiarism — which we can now nicely call interpolation, planned or otherwise — and what is fair game. As is often noted, there are 12 notes on the Western scale, which makes for a finite world of possibilities when it comes to quick hooks. I was intrigued by seeing references come up to the video where Charlie Puth shares his theory of what constitutes “interpolation”: up to four successive shared notes is fair game, he argues, but when you get to five, that’s when it’s time to share credit. Puth’s four-notes-or-less thesis has no legal standing — he just made it up — but it’s as good an argument as any to start or further these conversations. One young woman who clearly knows some music theory put up a video putting the melody of “Boston” up against “Stick Season” for comparison, finding that, once you transpose keys, Lefty’s song fails the Puth test for claiming originality. In the end, for the general public, it comes down less to rules about notes and bars than “I know it when I hear it.” And they know Kahan’s season of the stick even when it’s moved down from Vermont to Massacusetts.
	

	But here’s the followup question not very many are asking: Should America — or the huge part of America that doesn’t think this is a big deal — be guilted into stopping loving “Boston,” or Lefty herself?

	If you’re not overly consumed with “eat the rich” sentiment, it’s easy to see why “Boston” has become one of the biggest hits of 2026, borrowed elements or not. If Kahan had freely given “Stick Season” as a gift and Lefty had acknowledged it at the very top, we might be marveling at how she had transformed an existing hit into a fresh one that, ultimately, has a very different mood, theme and outcome. Music is always being adapted in alchemical ways, in ways that copyright lawyers can’t always comprehend and shouldn’t always constrain. The sin of “Boston” lie more in the lack of being completely unfront than in it being a bad song on its own admittedly compromised merits.

	It’s also a bit scary seeing how some of the sentiment out there has grown darker way beyond the bounds of what should be acceptable even in snarky circles. If anyone wants to call her Stella Thefty, fine. But closing circles around who and what should be a part of country music is an unfortunate byproduct of the singer’s background or credit issues. And if you really go down the rabbit hole of comments about the controversy, you’ll run into a world of antisemitism that is truly frightening (but to be expected). We’ll leave that at that.

	Here’s the argument in favor of “Boston,” unpopular as it might be right now: It’s winning because it’s winsome. Hearing Lefty sing “I like it when you’re nice to me” is the kind of bold, simple statement that transcends great lyricism — it’s heartwarming in the most basic kind of human way, stripping away all the other dross. Seeing Lefty scrunch up her face in delight at being desirable to a boyfriend is what the up side of pop is all about. Whatever anyone might have to say about her vocals, they’re appealing because her light rasp has a naturalness to it we rarely hear on the radio. Lefty became a newly minted star not because of her privilege but because she exudes approachability, even more so than a lot of country singers who came up from nothing. It’s not her fault, and maybe not her own doing, really, that she seems… nice. That can go a long way in 2026.
	

	But we can’t undo the layers of filters we see these things through, so appreciating “Boston” will never seem uncomplicated, and maybe the same goes for Lefty herself. She’s unlikely to ever give her family fortune away, but she can come back with a song that makes as indelible an impression as “Boston” while striking everyone with its originality… in theory, if not in likelihood. America does love a redemption story. But, to paraphrase a famous line from Flannery O’Connor’s “Wise Blood,” maybe nobody with a No. 2 hit that just won’t quit needs to be redeemed.

title: Pro-Paramount Group Uses AI to Pressure Rob Bonta to Drop Antitrust Case
description: A group supporting the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger is using artificial intelligence to help pressure California Attorney General Rob Bonta to drop
body:
A group supporting the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger is using artificial intelligence to help pressure California Attorney General Rob Bonta to drop his antitrust lawsuit.

	The group, which uses the neutral-sounding name Neighbors for Strong Communities, uses AI to craft letters that are sent to Bonta’s office, but says that the senders are all real people.

	“Anyone should be able to tell their story, and we use tech to make it easy for them,” said Tanner Kelly, the group’s co-founder. “Nothing we do is AI-generated. It’s AI-assisted. It’s a real person telling a story.”
	

	The group is also planning a press conference Thursday outside the Paramount gates to raise alarms about what would happen if the studio leaves California. CEO David Ellison has threatened to leave the state if no deal is reached by Oct. 1, when the company will begin to owe a $7 million-per-day ticking fee to Warner Bros. investors.


	Kelly declined to disclose the group’s donors, but denied the allegation that the group is a Paramount “astroturf” campaign — i.e., an artificial grassroots effort funded by a corporation.

	“This is an independent campaign. It’s not being run by Paramount,” he said. “We have not received any direct funding from Paramount.”

	Asked if he had received indirect funding from Paramount, he said he was not aware of it. 

	“As a general policy, we don’t disclose our donors. We comply with all reporting requirements,” he said. “We want to be able to attract donors to our [nonprofit] (c)4. Out of respect for the people who want to contribute, we don’t make it public.”
	

	Paramount declined to comment.

	Kelly is a registered lobbyist who also founded Influent, a vendor that uses AI to generate personalized letters to policymakers, in lieu of old-fashioned form letters. In a LinkedIn post last year, he wrote that he was using AI to help Fortune 100 companies “mobilize real, persuasive grassroots movements at scale.”

	AI-generated influence campaigns have been a controversial subject in California. In July, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a bill, AB 1736, that prohibits “lobbyist employers” from using fake comments to influence political outcomes.

	Influent’s website stresses that it relies on “real people,” and argues that it empowers them “to share their stories with on-message and persuasive materials that move decision-makers to action.” The company collects five-minute surveys from individuals and then turns them into advocacy letters, which the sender must approve before it is delivered.

	“Generic astroturf form letters are destined for the trash bin,” the company says on its website. “Every Influent letter, Tweet, phone call, and message is tailored to the individual — each one unique, reflecting the authentic voice of its sender.”

	Neighbors for Strong Communities, which was incorporated in Washington, D.C., in June, has also worked on a campaign against data centers and for Flock Safety, the surveillance camera company. Influent’s other co-founder, Nate Saletan, is also a director of Neighbors for Strong Communities, according to its incorporation filing.

	In the case of Paramount, Kelly said the group has mobilized 2,000 people, and has generated 1,000 calls to Bonta’s office. He said that AI was being used only for the letters, and not for the phone calls or other forms of outreach.

	The group is recording video testimonials from entertainment workers who say they fear the job impact if Paramount leaves California. The group made several of them available for interviews with Variety in advance of the press conference.

	“This is really scary,” said Ilona Roytman, a hair stylist who is involved in the campaign. “If they go away, a lot more people are going to lose their jobs.”

	Avrielle Corti, an actor and voice-over artist, said she, too, has concerns about Paramount moving out of state.
	

	“Taking Paramount out of California is like taking the Golden Gate Bridge and putting it in Nebraska,” she said.

	Dani Kelly, who runs a podcast studio in Chatsworth, has also provided a testimonial for the group and has posted on her social media about it.

	“L.A. was built by the studios,” she told Variety. “They are the hearts of L.A. Once they leave, there will be a ripple effect.”

	Kelly, who is no relation to the group’s co-founder, said that she was unaware of any AI component in the campaign.

	“We are legit people,” she said. “It’s not AI. I’m not a robot. Everybody behind the scenes are not robots.”

	The Committee for the First Amendment, which opposes the merger, called Neighbors for Strong Communities an “astroturf” campaign last month, after the latter group sent out text messages supporting the deal.

	“How do you call something ‘astroturf’ when it’s driven by real people?” Tanner Kelly asked. “The claim that this is astroturf is an attempt to silence real people who are worried about jobs going away because they don’t agree with them politically.”

	Roger Neal, a publicist who is helping with the press conference, argued that the antitrust case is politically motivated.

	“They don’t like the fact that a conservative family owns a studio in Hollywood,” he said. “So what if there’s one studio that has conservative ownership? So what?”

title: Dolly Parton's Hollywood Star Damaged After Flowers Stolen, Name Scratched
description:
Dolly Parton
                          Hollywood Walk of Fame Star Vandalized
body:
Dolly Parton
                          Hollywood Walk of Fame Star Vandalized
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 1, 2026
                            11:44 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Repairs are underway at Dolly Parton's star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame after a fan reported it was scratched up ... one week after the country music icon's death ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            Video captured by KNX shows crews working to replace the star after Dolly's name was scratched off. The star was dedicated in her honor in 1984.
      
    
      
      Repairs are underway at Dolly Parton's star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame after it was vandalized. Video on social media showed Parton's name scratched off. No word on any suspects, but has anyone seen Jolene lately? pic.twitter.com/2WAuvb7dEJ
              @knxnews
          
  
    
            Ana Martinez, a spokesperson for the Hollywood Chamber of Commerce, tells TMZ ... Dolly's star already had cracks in it, and the chamber had scheduled it to be repaired Tuesday. Martinez tells us a fan reported last night that someone had stolen flowers from the star and scratched it up.
      

                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            As we reported ... Dolly died last Tuesday at 80 following a brief battle with cancer. She was surrounded by loved ones at Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville when she passed.
      
    
            Dolly's death came as a shock even to people close to her who knew she'd been dealing with health problems.

body:
'Wife Swap' Star Princess
                          Found Dead At 53 Inside A Sober House
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 1, 2026
                            11:30 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    The "Wife Swap" star known as Princess has been found dead inside a sober house in Pennsylvania -- this according to the county coroner.Luzerne County Coroner Dion Fernandes tells TMZ ... Princess, whose real name is James Cuda, was discovered inside a sober home in Wilkes-Barre on Sunday afternoon. Fernandes said no foul play was suspected and Princess' cause of death was pending toxicology results.
    
          Waiting for your permission to load TikTok Post.
      
    
            Princess was best known for his memorable 2013 episode of "Wife Swap," in which he was cast as a gay nanny who traveled from Las Vegas to an Amish farm in Michigan.
      

            When he arrived, the Christian farm owners and their 6 kids suddenly turned nasty, saying gay people were disgusting before tossing Princess out of their house. The internet went wild over the episode, which became one of the most compelling in "Wife Swap" history.
      
    
        Waiting for your permission to load the Instagram Media.
      
    
            Marissa Zdazinsky, Princess' close friend and "Wife Swap" castmate, posted about his death on Instagram, calling it "the saddest moment of my life." Marissa also said Princess was battling alcohol issues and she and her husband tried to help him through his issues, saying that it wasn't easy.
      
    
            Princess was 53.
      
    
            RIP

title: 14-Year-Old Wanted for Murdering Her Baby, on Run With Father Who Allegedly Got Her Pregnant

                          Wanted For Her Newborn's Murder
body:
14-Year-Old Girl
                          Wanted For Her Newborn's Murder
                          Dad Allegedly Fathered Baby
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 1, 2026
                            10:36 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 1, 2026
                                11:55 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            A 14-year-old murder suspect is on the run with her own father ... and cops say he's also the father of her dead newborn baby.
      
    
            Authorities in Monterey County, California are searching for the teen and 38-year-old Sergio Galves Perez after "Baby Angelita" was found dead along a roadside on Aug. 1 ... with her umbilical cord still attached and signs of trauma.
      
    
            Investigators say Perez allegedly impregnated his daughter when she was just 13. He's now wanted on several charges -- including incest -- while the girl is wanted for murder.
      

            Sheriff Tina Nieto says the teenager may also be in danger ... stressing that despite being a suspect, she's also a victim.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Perez's wife, Ofelia Garcia Ortega, has already been arrested and charged with child endangerment ... after investigators linked a vehicle in the case back to the family.
      
    
            Authorities are asking for help finding the father and daughter as the investigation into Baby Angelita's death continues.

title: Brittany Cartwright to Jax Taylor: Keep Your New Girlfriend Lori Away From Our Son!!!
description:
Brittany Cartwright
                          Warns Ex-Jax To Keep GF Lori Away From Their Son
body:
Brittany Cartwright
                          Warns Ex-Jax To Keep GF Lori Away From Their Son
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 1, 2026
                            10:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            "Vanderpump Rules" alum Brittany Cartwright berated her estranged husband, Jax Taylor, for allegedly bringing his new girlfriend, Lori Krebs, around their kids, TMZ has learned. 
      
    
            TMZ obtained messages Jax and Brittany exchanged on July 15, 2026, one day after we broke the story that Jax and his publicist, Lori, were hooking up. Brittany used to be represented by Lori before the news broke. 
      
    
            Jax wrote, “Your sick brain thought it was okay to have a random guy sleep in the same house with my son ... a guy you had to pay to be your boyfriend non the less.”
      

            Brittany fired back, telling Jax he signed a court document stating he wouldn’t bring any new woman around their son for the first 6 months of seeing someone. “You broke the law Lori is to never be around my son.” 
      
    
            “You have crossed the line having my son around her,” he said. “If it happens again he will be taken out of your home. Do not contact me you will see him next weekend.” 
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Jax told his ex that Lori had been around since he was born. “I am also telling my lawyer if you don’t allow me to take him to Michigan he will never set foot in Kentucky again.”
      
    
            “You are not to have anyone around Cruz including her,” Brittany said as she ended the convo.

title: 'Dutton Ranch' Feud Between Cole Hauser, Taylor Sheridan Nearly Comes to Blows
description:
Cole Hauser & Taylor Sheridan
                          Real-Life Ranch Showdown ...
body:
Cole Hauser & Taylor Sheridan
                          Real-Life Ranch Showdown ...
                          California Vs. Texas Beef
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 1, 2026
                            9:45 AM PDT
                                                                      |
                                                                Updated 
                                  September 1, 2026
                                11:52 AM PDT
                                    
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Rip Wheeler's got beef with the boss ... and this Dutton Ranch feud has apparently come damn close to getting physical.
      
    
            Cole Hauser and Taylor Sheridan have reportedly been butting heads behind the scenes for years, with the Daily Mail reporting one clash during "Yellowstone" nearly turned into a fistfight.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            That wouldn't exactly be a first ... Hauser previously revealed he and Sheridan actually fought the second time they ever met ... before eventually becoming friends.
      

            But the tension apparently never fully disappeared.
      
    
            The Mail's sources describe the two as total opposites -- Hauser the laid-back California guy, Sheridan the hard-charging Texas cowboy -- and say they've repeatedly clashed.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Things got messier in 2023, when Sheridan sued Hauser over their competing cowboy coffee brands ... accusing Hauser's Free Rein of using branding too similar to his Bosque Ranch company. They settled the case privately in 2024.
      
    
            More recently, Hauser publicly complained about Sheridan not being around much for the first season of "Dutton Ranch," saying production was a challenge.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            According to the Mail, those comments didn't sit well with Sheridan ... with one source saying they made it sound like there were problems behind the scenes.
      
    
            Hauser has also griped about filming in North Texas, where the brutal heat made it tough to keep on the roughly 25 pounds he normally gains to play Rip.
      
    
            Still, Hauser reportedly has plenty of respect for Sheridan and knows "Yellowstone" turned Rip Wheeler into his biggest role.
      
    
            California and Texas may be at war ... but for now, they're still sharing the ranch.
